note_on_method: Nobody working on this has played on these courts. Every count, address, price and opening time below is taken from the City of Mesa's own pages - the Mesa Tennis & Pickleball Center's facility page, and the park pages for Kleinman and Chaparral. Mesa publishes a great deal about its parks and very little about its pickleball, and the gap between those two things is the shape of this page. Six more Mesa parks say the words "Pickleball Court" without ever saying how many, and they are named at the bottom rather than quietly left out.

slots.parking: Mesa publishes nothing at all about parking at any of these three venues. Not a lot, not a space count, not a fee, not a permit - the word does not appear on the Center's page or on either park page, and this site does not fill that in from a satellite photo. What can be said is what the City does publish about getting in the gate, and it differs sharply between the two kinds of venue here. The Mesa Tennis & Pickleball Center is a staffed facility with a front desk: the City asks you to "check-in at the front desk prior to your reservation to check-in and get your court assignment number", and warns that "Court fees must be paid inside pro shop before using the facility. Unauthorized use of the facility is considered trespassing." So arriving at the Center is a transaction, not a walk-up. Kleinman Park and Chaparral Park are ordinary municipal parks open sunrise to 10 p.m. with no gate and no desk, and at Chaparral the City's own note tells you the one thing you must bring: a net. Kleinman is the larger site of the two, with a softball complex, ramadas both reservable and not, restrooms and an unpaved walking path, which usually implies a car park; the City does not say so, so neither do we.
slots.peak_hours: For once there is a real answer, and it comes from the operator rather than from guesswork: the Mesa Tennis & Pickleball Center closes in the middle of the day. Its published hours are 5:30 a.m. to 11:30 a.m. every day, and then again 5:00 p.m. to 10:00 p.m. Monday through Friday only. On Saturday and Sunday it does not reopen in the evening at all. That is a schedule shaped by Arizona, and it tells you more about when to turn up than any crowd estimate would: there is no such thing as a lunchtime game at the Center, and at the weekend there is no such thing as an evening one. It also means the twenty-one courts are available for about six hours on a weekday and six hours on a Saturday, which is a smaller window than the raw court count suggests. The City adds one further warning in its own words - "Tournaments, league and lesson programming, special events, or maintenance may limit court space for the general public" - so the published hours are the outer limit rather than a promise. Courts can be booked online up to two weeks in advance, and league reservations are priced separately, both of which point the same way: at the Center, planning ahead is the norm and turning up hopefully is not. Kleinman and Chaparral are the opposite arrangement. Both are open sunrise to 10 p.m., neither charges anything the City discloses, and Mesa publishes nothing whatsoever about when either one is busy.
slots.surface_condition: Mesa states a surface for none of these courts, which is the ordinary case in this directory rather than a failing peculiar to Mesa. What the City does say, at one venue, is more useful than a surface note would be. Chaparral Park's entry reads in full: "Pickleball Court (1 lined court shared with basketball use, bring your own portable net)". Every part of that is worth reading twice. It is one court, not several; it is lines painted onto a basketball court rather than a pickleball court; the basketball use has not gone anywhere, so the court is shared in the literal sense of somebody else possibly being on it; and no net is provided, which is unusual enough to be the single most practical fact on this page. At the other end of the city, the Center's twenty-one courts are described by the City as "lighted pickleball courts", listed alongside sixteen lighted tennis courts and four sand volleyball courts at a facility with a pro shop, ball machines for hire and a rule that non-marking shoes must be worn. Nothing states what any of it is made of. Kleinman sits between the two and says least: four courts, counted, and no description of them at all.
slots.local_scene: Twenty-six verified courts at three venues, and twenty-one of them are in one place. The Mesa Tennis & Pickleball Center holds the largest single-venue pickleball count anywhere in this directory, and it is a genuine racquet-sports centre rather than a park with lines on it - staffed, ticketed, floodlit, with a pro shop and a teaching professional, and a rule that private coaching for money is prohibited unless the City authorised it. Play there costs $9.00 per court per hour before 5 p.m. and $13.00 after. That is the Mesa scene as the City documents it: one substantial paid facility, and then a long tail of neighbourhood courts it barely describes. The tail is genuinely long, and this is the honest shape of the city. Mesa's parks pages carry the words "Pickleball Court" at six more parks - Gene Autry, Christopher J. Brady, Red Mountain, Augusta Ranch, Sheepherders and Washington - and not one of them states a number. Brady Park is reservable online and the City publishes a weekly calendar for each of its courts individually; Red Mountain and Augusta Ranch have lines on a basketball court and ask you to bring a net. Every one of those is a place people plainly play. None of them can be published here, because a count is what this site requires and Mesa has not written one down. So the real number of pickleball courts in Mesa is comfortably higher than twenty-six, and this page will not guess at how much higher. Mesa is the second Arizona city here after Scottsdale, and the second in Maricopa County.

best_for.heading: Best if you want a real game on a proper court
best_for.text: The Mesa Tennis & Pickleball Center has twenty-one lighted pickleball courts, the largest count at any single venue on this site. It is staffed, it has a pro shop and ball machines to rent, and you can book a court online up to a fortnight ahead. It also costs money and keeps unusual hours: $9.00 per court per hour before 5 p.m., $13.00 after, open mornings 5:30 to 11:30 every day and evenings 5:00 to 10:00 on weekdays only.

best_for.heading: Best if you just want to turn up
best_for.text: Kleinman Park has four pickleball courts in a park that is open sunrise to 10 p.m., with restrooms, ramadas and a softball complex on the same site. The City states no charge for the courts, though it does not state that they are free either. Courts here are booked through the Tennis & Pickleball Center if you want one reserved.

best_for.heading: Best only if you own a net
best_for.text: Chaparral Park is one court, and the City is unusually honest about what that means: lines on a basketball court, shared with basketball, and no net provided. If you have a portable net in the boot this is a perfectly good hit close to central Mesa. If you do not, it is not a pickleball court that day.

faqs.q: How many pickleball courts does Mesa have?
faqs.a: Many more than we can verify. We have confirmed 26 across three venues: twenty-one at the Mesa Tennis & Pickleball Center, four at Kleinman Park and one at Chaparral Park. Six further Mesa parks list pickleball courts without stating a number, so the true figure is higher and the City has not published it.

faqs.q: Which Mesa venue has the most courts?
faqs.a: The Mesa Tennis & Pickleball Center, at 4125 E McKellips Rd, with twenty-one lighted pickleball courts. That is the largest single-venue count anywhere in this directory.

faqs.q: Is it free to play in Mesa?
faqs.a: Not at the Center, which charges $9.00 per court per hour before 5 p.m. and $13.00 after, and states that fees must be paid at the pro shop before you use the facility. At Kleinman and Chaparral the City publishes no price at all, which is not the same as publishing that they are free, so this site does not describe any Mesa venue as free.

The Center's are: the City calls them "21 lighted pickleball courts" in its own words. At Kleinman and Chaparral it is not stated. Mesa marks lighting by writing it into the amenity name, and at both parks a lighted basketball or volleyball court sits in the same list while the pickleball entry carries no such mark. That is a hint, not a statement, so this site records lighting as unverified at both.

faqs.q: Are these courts indoor or outdoor?
faqs.a: Mesa never says, about any of them. It is the one thing this otherwise detailed operator leaves out entirely, and it is why Mesa has no indoor or outdoor filter page on this site while smaller cities do.

faqs.q: Do I need to bring a net?
faqs.a: At Chaparral Park, yes - the City says so: "bring your own portable net". At the Center, no; it is a full facility with permanent courts. At Kleinman the City does not say.

At the Center, yes, online up to two weeks ahead, with longer notice handled by a request form. Kleinman Park's courts are also reservable, and the City directs those bookings through the Tennis & Pickleball Center. Chaparral is not listed as reservable.

faqs.q: Why are only three Mesa venues listed when the City names nine?
faqs.a: Because six of the nine state no court count. Every Mesa park page carries a Features list, and "Pickleball Court" appears on it as a label printed identically whether a park has one court or six. Sheepherders Park proves the point on a single page, writing "Pickleball Courts" in one list and "Pickleball Court" in another without ever giving a number. This site publishes a stated count or nothing.

faqs.q: Why is Gene Autry Park not listed separately?
faqs.a: Because the Mesa Tennis & Pickleball Center stands inside it and shares its street address - the park page prints 4125 E Mckellips Rd and the Center's page prints 4125 E McKellips Rd. Listing both would put two venues at one address. The park also states no pickleball count of its own, which would have excluded it anyway.
